data.summary: sessions.capture_prompt dedupes a harness double fire by asking whether the same words were recorded for the session within DOUBLE_FIRE_S (3 s) of NOW, where now is after the hook process started, imported ddflow, loaded config and read the log. On a loaded machine that startup alone can exceed the window, so the second copy of one firing is recorded as a second prompt. Probe: a second 'hooks prompt' whose startup is delayed by DOUBLE_FIRE_S+1 s (sitecustomize sleep) records 2 session.prompt events (tests/test_prompt_autocapture.py::test_a_copy_slow_to_start_is_still_the_same_firing fails 2 == 1). Root cause of the full-suite flake B7e6f1998c8. Fix: measure the age from when the hook process was started.
data.title: prompt hook counts its own startup against the double-fire window

data.claim: The heartbeat revival renews the lease on the claim's own ttl_s (1 s, from DDFLOW_LEASE_TTL_S=1 at claim time) with grace_s = 0, so the revived lease lapses again ~1 s later; when the bare-env hook subprocess starts more than 1 s after the revival (a loaded machine), check-commit finds the lease lapsed and prints 'not covered'.

chunk_findings.detail: The helper does not make the revived lease *correct*; it makes every lease that lapsed up to an hour ago count as live. With `[lease].grace_s = 3600`, the hook's "am I covered" check adds a one-hour grace window to the expiry, so a lease that lapsed (or was never renewed) is still treated as live and covering. That removes the test's ability to detect the very regression it is supposed to pin down: give `heartbeat T1` a revival that returns `O.OK` but does not actually extend the revived lease (e.g. it only rewrites the globs, or the lease keeps its original expiry). The lease is lapsed by ~1 s, well inside the 3600 s grace, so `_hook_after_revival(..., pause_s=1.5)` and the non-pause test both still see `src/a.py` as covered, `"not covered"` is absent, and both pass. With the original `grace_s = 0` the same broken-revival input fails the assertion, so the change silently drops coverage of the lease-lifetime/revival expiry bug instead of fixing it; any real environment where the lease lifetime is short (the claim TTL case this bug is about) still produces the "not covered" hook failure the test was meant to guard. The comment claims "empty or wrong revived globs still fail," but a correct-glob / unrefreshed-expiry revival is exactly the case that no longer fails.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_claim_globs.py:_hook_after_revival (the `grace_s = 3600` rewrite)

chunk_findings.detail: The helper rewrites `[lease].grace_s` from `0` to `3600` in `config.toml` before the hook runs. A grace period is precisely the window in which an already-expired lease is still treated as covering, so with `grace_s = 3600` the revived lease is "covered" for ~1 hour no matter what TTL the revival renewed it on. The new regression test is named `test_a_hook_slower_than_the_claims_ttl_still_sees_the_revived_claim`, i.e. it claims to prove that a hook starting after the claim's 1 s TTL still sees the claim, but the `grace_s = 3600` rewrite removes the temporal constraint entirely: change the `heartbeat` line to do nothing (or renew on a 0 s TTL) while keeping the `grace_s = 3600` write, and the test still exits 0 with no "not covered" as long as the path is within the pre-existing claim's globs — the assertion is satisfied by grace, not by any renewal. The only thing the test actually exercises is glob matching, which the preceding `test_after_a_revival_the_hook_accepts_a_path_the_claim_covers` / `_lease_globs` assertions already cover. Consequently the failure mode Be33d572ada describes (revival renewing on the claim's own short TTL, so a hook >1 s later reads "not covered") is not guarded: reintroduce that behaviour with the production grace (`0`/small) and the test still cannot see it, because the test itself rewrites the config to a value that masks it. To actually test the named scenario the helper must leave `grace_s` at its real value and assert the revived lease's own TTL/expiry was extended (or the revival must be fixed to renew on a non-claim TTL).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_claim_globs.py:_hook_after_revival → test_a_hook_slower_than_the_claims_ttl_still_sees_the_revived_claim

chunk_findings.detail: The fix converts the dedupe window from "record-time minus record-time" to "second firing's process-start minus first record's timestamp", i.e. it forgives the *second* hook's startup but silently assumes the *first* hook logged the instant it was fired. Let `a` be when the first hook process started, `s1` its own startup latency before it appends the `session.prompt` event, so the event `ts` is `r1 = a + s1`. Let `b` be when the second hook process is fired. `_recorded_recently` now reports `duplicate` iff `b - r1 <= DOUBLE_FIRE_S`, i.e. `(b - a) - s1 <= 3`, i.e. a genuine gap `b - a` is swallowed whenever `b - a <= 3 + s1`. The old code compared `r2 - r1`, which for equal start-ups was exactly the intended 3 s. So the effective window is widened by the first hook's startup latency — precisely the quantity B72b9ab33fc says a loaded machine stretches arbitrarily. Concretely: first hook fired at `a=0`, machine is loaded so it takes `s1=5 s` to log at `r1=5`; the operator then genuinely sends the same text again and the harness fires the second hook at `b=8` (`Δ=8 s`, clearly not a double-fire). `_age_s(ev.ts, b) = 8 - 5 = 3 <= 3`, so `capture_prompt` returns `"duplicate"` and the second, legitimate prompt is dropped, whereas the pre-change code (`r2 - r1 = 3 + s2 > 3`) recorded it. `HOOK_START_MAX_S` does not bound this: the widening is caused by the *first* process's startup, while the second process is fresh (`now - fired_at = s2`, small), so the clamp never engages. Since the whole premise of the change is that hook start-up can be multiple seconds on a loaded machine, an operator repeating the same prompt within `3 + s1` seconds is now silently discarded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py:325 (`capture_prompt`, the `fired` / `_recorded_recently(..., now=fired)` lines)

chunk_findings.detail: The new test simulates a slow-starting hook by putting a `sitecustomize.py` that sleeps `DOUBLE_FIRE_S + 1` seconds first on `PYTHONPATH`, then asserts the second copy is deduped. That only works where the dedupe reference is derived from the kernel-recorded process start (the Linux `/proc/self/stat` path described in the intent). On any non-Linux platform — and per the intent those fall back to "now" — the fallback timestamp is taken after `sitecustomize` has already slept, i.e. at `first_event_time + ~(DOUBLE_FIRE_S + 1)`. Concretely, on macOS/Windows: first `_hook` records `session.prompt` at `T1`; the second `_hook` blocks 4 s in `sitecustomize`, then computes its window start as ≈ `T1 + 4.x`; `4.x > DOUBLE_FIRE_S (3)` so no dedupe occurs, the second event is written, and the final assertion `len(_events(repo, "session.prompt")) == 1` fails. The test carries no `skipif(not linux)`/`/proc` guard, so it is a deterministic failure on the very platforms the change's fallback branch exists to support; the sleep must either be gated to the /proc-capable path or the test marked Linux-only.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_prompt_autocapture.py:test_a_copy_slow_to_start_is_still_the_same_firing

chunk_findings.detail: The hook now stamps every capture with the *process* start rather than the event time. The only guard against this being wrong is the clamp `fired_at = max(process_start, now - HOOK_START_MAX_S)`, but that clamp does nothing for the first 30 s of the process's life: throughout that window `process_started_at()` returns a constant. So if the harness does not spawn a fresh process per prompt — e.g. a session-scoped/persistent hook runner, a daemon that drains queued hook payloads, or (as the change's own comment anticipates) an in-process caller — then every capture in that process gets the *same* `fired_at`. Two genuinely distinct prompts in the same session must then compare as `Δ = 0 s`, which is inside DOUBLE_FIRE_S = 3, and the second is silently discarded as a "double fire". Concrete input: process starts at T; prompt A arrives at T+0.2 s (recorded with `fired_at = T`); the user re-submits the same text at T+25 s (also recorded with `fired_at = T`). `|T - T| = 0 < 3`, so the second legitimate prompt is swallowed, whereas the pre-change code compared check times (25 s apart) and recorded it. The 30 s bound only makes `fired_at` start moving after the process is 30 s old, so the window of over-dedupe is precisely the first 30 s of any reused process.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:813 (`fired_at=S.process_started_at()`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new comparison is `fired - ts_first <= DOUBLE_FIRE_S`, where `ts_first` is when the first copy *appended* its event, not when the first copy was *fired*. Those differ by the first hook's own startup/imports/log-read delay, i.e. exactly the quantity this change is premised on being able to exceed 3 s on a loaded machine. So the real dedupe window becomes `DOUBLE_FIRE_S + d_first`, where `d_first` is the first hook's recording lag, and any legitimate repeat prompt fired inside that enlarged window is silently dropped instead of recorded. Concretely: first hook starts at t=0 and is slow, recording its event at t=8 (`d_first=8`, the very load condition B72b9ab33fc targets). The operator then genuinely retypes the same text 10 s later; the harness fires a second hook at t=10, which starts and checks at t=16 (`fired=10`). `_age_s(ev.ts=8, now=10)` returns `-2`, which is `<= 3`, so `capture_prompt` returns `"duplicate"` and the second prompt is never logged — even though the two firings are 10 s apart, far outside the documented 3 s window ("a longer window would eat an operator who really types 'continue' twice"). The old code computed `check_time - ts_first = 16 - 8 = 8 > 3` and recorded it, so this is a regression introduced by keying the window off the *record* time of the earlier event rather than off the earlier *firing*; the window is also unbounded on the future side (`ev.ts > fired` yields a negative age, always treated as recent), so a first hook that is delayed past a later same-text prompt can even refuse to record its own earlier prompt.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py:171 (`_recorded_recently`) / `capture_prompt` (`now=fired`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new test hard-codes a Linux-only fix behaviour into an unguarded test. The fix only recovers the hook's true start instant from `/proc/self/stat` on Linux; per the stated design, on every other platform the start time falls back to `now`. On macOS/Windows the artificial delay injected by `sitecustomize.py` (`time.sleep(DOUBLE_FIRE_S + 1)`) therefore happens *before* the start instant is sampled, so by the time the hook runs its dedupe check the previous `session.prompt` event is already ~4.1 s old — more than `DOUBLE_FIRE_S == 3` — and the second copy is recorded as a distinct event. The test then fails on `assert len(_events(repo, "session.prompt")) == 1` with 2 != 1, on exactly the developer machines this project is likely developed on. The test needs a `sys.platform == "linux"` / `/proc` skip guard (or a portable way to obtain the process start time) before it can be a regression test for B7e6f1998c8.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_prompt_autocapture.py:137 (`test_a_copy_slow_to_start_is_still_the_same_firing`)
